blocks.x: This is an interview being recorded at 600 Charter Street, September the 26th, 1959 and this is Dick Allen talking. What's your name on? Oh, Bill Ruffles here.
Okay, and who are we talking? And Bailey.
Yeah, and what's your full name, Bailey?
Andrew Bailey.
Mm-hmm, and if you don't mind me asking a personal question, what's your birthday, Bailey?
18, July the 8th, July 1899, 25th.
25th.
Mm-hmm.
And let's see, did you have any musicians in your family, Bailey?
No, no musician at all.
Mm-hmm. And you never did play yourself?
Never did play. Used to go to dances.
Mm-hmm, see?
Loved music.
Mm-hmm. Well now, what was the first music you remember or singing or anything as a kid?
Well, it was Wood and Joe. Used to play at the place of Burns Hall for parties on Sundays. Mm-hmm.
Would that be in the afternoon or night?
That'd be at night. Mm-hmm. From 8 till 8.
By the way, where were you raised? What part of town?
New Orleans. New Orleans, Louisiana in the 7 Ward. Pog and Burry.
What streets?
Pog and Burry. Oh, yeah. Used to be Bourbon once, but they changed it to Pogger. Mm-hmm.
I see. Now, Bailey, did you hear anybody around your house singing or in church or anything?
Well, I used to go to plenty of concerts at churches. Used to have concerts them days. Mm-hmm. Yeah, way back in 18, around 19, up, around 1914.
And what would happen at these concerts?
Well, no more than singing and entertaining, joking. No, it's happening.
Do they have any certain night, or are they like on a Sunday or Monday or any certain day?
No, not for the church concert. Being a weekday, like on Monday nights, Saturday nights. Yeah.
Well, do you remember anybody in particular that'd be at these church concerts?
Well, it's been so long, I forgot some of the folks in Young Wooden and got married since them days.
Back to Wooden Joe. Do you remember any of the guys that ever played with Wooden Joe in that band?
Well, I just can't call his name now. I just remember his name. Yeah, I used to know two, three of them used to play with him.
How big a band did he have? How many instruments?
Well, he had about six, seven people with him.
What was the featured instruments in those days, Bailey?
Well, it was the cornet, violin, clarinet, an old violin, and drum.
Do you remember any violin players by name?
Well, at this moment I couldn't tell you, but I could get them named. Yeah, well we'll do it again. Yeah.
Now what about trumpet players? You named several of them to me a minute ago. Who were some of the outstanding?
Well, the outstanding was Emmanuel Parais, one of the best cornet players in the New Lane.
Do you remember where he lived about? Is it near your house?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. He lived down the 7 Ward, right on the 8 Court, around the corner, about two squares from my house. He used to live.
Did you hear him in parades or didn't they?

Yeah, I heard him in parades, yeah. He heard him in parades, one of the wonderful cornet players was going. And that's way back in 1960. Did you used to second line? Yeah, I used to second line. Yeah, and the second line I used to do.
Can you tell us some more about those parades? What kind of organizations put them on and where they had them?
Well, they had them from different organizations, like some of the clubs had them. Like the Zulus and Square Deal. They had them, they used to have them.
What would happen at those parades?

Well, when they used to have parades, plenty of fights would go on, but the law would be there to back them back on the second line. Well, they wouldn't hurt each other much. No, no, they wouldn't hurt nobody. They would, especially when they would have parades, going to cemeteries. Well, it used to be a little better than going to parades, real parades, than going to a funeral. But when they would have a funeral, going to the cemetery, they'd be playing plenty of hymn. But when they're coming back, they're playing nothing but the right time. Everybody would be there dancing, coming back.
But when they fight like that, what did they fight with?

Well, some of them fight with their hands. They used to call it different wards. Some fellows wouldn't want this man to come in his ward like the 7th, 8th, 9th ward. They wouldn't want them to come in their ward. They try when they get in their ward, they go to fighting them on their cell. And they go back in their ward, they run them, try to stay away from each one's ward.
What else would they use besides their fists?
That's all. I never known of them to get hoisted.
Somebody told me once they used to have sticks or something like cream sticks, every kind of those?
Well, some of them would have broomsticks, but they'll all be right there on them. They'll all be right there, no, no.
Well, would they hire policemen to follow the parades or would they just...
Yeah, yeah, they'd have policemen behind the parades. Yeah, they'd have police behind the parades.
When did they have most of the parades, any certain day?
Well, yeah, same time of the year they would have them. Different organization would have parades. Same time of the year.
Do you remember the funerals? Were there many funerals with music?
Yeah, yeah, because I was into myself with music. Yeah, I used to be in society with music. Plenty of funerals with music.
Well...
Yeah.
What societies were you a member of?

Well, used to... Well, when I was in, I was in the... Well, I know some of the clubs like the Bar Day, you know, all them there, but I wasn't in their society. Mm-hmm. Yeah, the... Plenty of society, charities, the liberty, all that.
Well, how did they work, those societies?

Well, like organization. Mm-hmm. When the people would die, they'd make a rent for the bar and the funeral and for the music. Where'd they get the money from? Well, they come from the society. Some of the family wouldn't want no music. But they thought they would get the money, they'd all get the money. But they would tax you for music. Tax the members for music when they want music. Plenty of them would have music. Some wouldn't want it.
Well, are those societies secret?
No. Well, no secret society. No secret society. There's benevolence. When you're sick and things. Takes you out. Buried.
Who can get in those societies? Anybody?
Oh, yeah, yeah. Mm-hmm. As long as you pay your dues. Yeah. That's for sick. Buried. Keep the corporation from taking care of you.
About how much were the dues? Was it every week or every month?

Every month. Every month. Sometimes twice a month. When it comes twice a month, that means quarterly. But monthly dues every month. But they have quarterly. Yeah. Like somewhere I would die, well, they're coming quarterly. Certain, you know, the charges for your quarterly. Yeah. But every month you had your dues to pay. About how much were the... Might be 75 cents. A month. Yeah. But sometimes you got quarterly. Might have two, three people die and you got to pay for your quarterly. Yeah. Charging more, 50 cents, 75 cents. Sometimes in my head, two, three people die right straight along. Come down to quarterly, as much as the monthly. Yeah. Society.
Did they charge much for those uniforms?
Well, what you mean, for the bands?
No, for the members.
Oh, no. That's what I'm telling you. It's always six bits, four bits, quarterly. But your society would be 75 cents a month. Well, who... That's your monthly.
Who do the uniforms belong to?

They don't have uniforms, our society. This... Well, yeah. It's like somebody die, they want you all in black. Yeah. You have to have your black clothes, blue's clothes. Yeah, that's your clothes. Mm-hmm. That's your own clothes.
Some of them, the masons have the little...
Oh, that's different. That's masons. No, no. Well, I wasn't... That was no masons. That's benevolent, call that.
But you didn't have any special kind of hats?
No, no, no. No, that's... That's mason heads, all that. Yeah. Mason heads, all that.
Where did the funerals, where did they bury most of the people in those days?
In the city. Remember which cemetery? Yeah, I know all of them. St. Rock, St. Louis, Hoax, that Girard, the Toadown. Oh, yeah. Old graveyard. Yeah. Plenty of them.
Now, where did the funerals, where did they usually meet? At an undertaker's parlor?
No, well, they missed at the home.
Or did they ever start out from your club, too?

Yeah, but most people be buried from the... They had the undertaker, they missed at the undertaker. But plenty of them days, they was at the house. They didn't have an undertaker, or they had the house. Like my folks today, we buried at the house. Don't see that much. Everybody at the undertaker. But these days, that pallet they want.
What does the club start mason from?
Well, they start right from the house.
They meet at the house.

That's right. Well, you know, they don't meet at the house. They meet at their hall. At their hall. Like they might have their hall at the Poison Vern, so they call them at Hall, Corporate. Well, they meet there and come to the house where the bar is at.
The band would pick you up at the hall.
At the house. At the house. Yeah.
The band would be at the house.

Yeah, at the house. The band would be at the house. All the members would be where the band would be at. And they meet the bar at the house. Then the undertaker would come along and everybody would go to the funeral. Well, we used to walk them days. They didn't have a lot of mobiles. And everybody would be glad to walk. And we all fall in line. The music played nothing but hymns. Going to the funeral. But when they come back, nothing but the right time.
What were some of the hymns they played?
Oh, most of all the old hymns was like Nero, My God to D. Yeah.
And what were some of the rag down numbers they played?
Oh, Tiger Rag. Jelly Roll. All that old time music.
That's coming back.
Yeah. Kick the Bucket. I've never heard that.
How does that go?
Oh, that's a dance. They're dancing and kicking their legs and everything.
That's a dance?
Yeah. Something like the hem kick? That's right. That's right. Kick the head. That's right. That's a dance.
Well, they had all kinds of dances.
Oh, yeah. They had these dances. They got all kinds of things. Like the Julie Buck, they didn't have them dance. They had the slew drag. The shim and all that. Kick the hem. Kick the bucket.
So, what did you like to dance?
Oh, I used to like the Tiger Rag.
I used to like that.

Yeah. What kind of dances did you do? Oh, I had to do two steps. Mostly two steps. Two steps and slow drag. Two steps and slow drag. Dance with all your people out and throw them out and come in. They ain't like that Junibug, you know. No, like they got today.
Did you ever dance any quadrilles?

Oh, no, but I used to look at them dance. I couldn't dance. I used to look at the folks dance there. Put all the ladies on one side. You on one side, you meet the lady. Come down the aisle. Yeah, that's old dances. Yeah.
About how many would take part in that?

Well, they have about 20 of them. 20 of them. You can be at a big dance when quadrilles come along. They just have people that really knows how to do that. Everybody that be like when they got at ragtime, everybody would dance together. When the quadrilles come, everybody looking at them people, search people among themselves that knows it. Some men on one side and the men on one side. Yeah. We'd be looking at them dancing. So a lot of people would watch. Yeah, plenty of prizes be given for that, them days. And they had the waltz, another dance I couldn't do. I could see it and look at the people doing what them days people used to know how to dance waltz. And they had prizes for that.
About the quadrilles, to interrupt you, did they have it a certain time each night?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, through the night they have it.
More than once?
Well, about two, three times it come along through the whole night. About two, three times it come along.
What years was that when they had the quadrilles?
Oh, that was way around, let me see, after September storm. That was way around 1918, right after September storm, 1915.
It lasted quite a while then, huh?
What, the ball?
The quadrilles, I mean it.
Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. It lasted about 15, 20 minutes until they played the music, played a tune.
What I mean is it lasted in the late years, pretty late then.
Oh yeah, 1918. A lot of people should remember that. Yeah, it ain't. Sound, it's long time, but it's 1918. Sure, like the September storm, I remember that good.
You remember that storm?

Sure, I used to wake at cloud cracker factory. They let us off at two o'clock, not stay in the 20-hundred block. Took me till nine o'clock to get home. Yeah, could make it. A lot of water? Waiting for the rain, yeah, plenty of water and plenty of building knocked down. Really? Plenty of building. Waste on the head had in history since I knew it. 1915, I don't want to see a storm like that no more. Waste on the other scene, knocked down churches. Or the Frank church, all back in town.
How many days did it start?

Starting in the morning then? Oh, starting in the morning. Well, that storm came up. That real wind started up around, started coming up around 11 o'clock. Around two o'clock the wind kept coming. When she really got laid, it was around eight, nine o'clock. And she was doing it. Yeah, terrible storm.
Is your house all right?
Yeah, my house was pretty good. Yeah, we had a nice little solid house.
Yeah, we had water in the streets almost over the whole city.

Oh yeah, yeah, some people had water almost gone in they do. All on ramp, part and scintillation. I'll never forget. All the wire fell down. There's a man who used to direct the people. You know, a special man, keep the people walking on the bank. I was going to kill myself running on the bank. The man just had to pull me back, shut me out in the street. You know, take the street, couldn't pass on the bank. That's the time they had to try laundry. That's old laundry they used to have around there. Try laundry.
Oh yeah. Did you hear much music before that storm? Do you remember any bands that played before that time?
Yeah, I remember bands when I couldn't go to dances. Yeah, I remember way back, way back to have dances. Around 1980 or 18, I think. But I couldn't go to dances then.
Did you know any of the guys' names?
Well, more than I heard them on late afterwards.
Yeah, which you didn't know their names then?

No, I didn't know their names. Just like Joe Oliver. I remember him. I didn't start going to his dance until the way around. Way around that Yelder Stone. I started to go to his dance. Because I used to go to most of them on carnival nights. I used to go to dances. Mardi Gras nights. Yeah, we was in short pants. We had to put long pants. Take my daddy pants and put it over our short pants. Because you couldn't let that children come in bald then day. The children come in bald at all.
How was the carnival in those days?
Oh, carnival was fine. Better than today. It was carnival then day. Today you had people walking. But them days you had nothing but maskers. But I masked twice and got set afire in monkeys.
You got set afire?

Yeah. You see them clothes they had this put a match. Oh yeah. Yeah, that's kind of clothes they had them days. You can't do that now with the clothes they had. You could be on the monkeys since you got all that fire. Like cotton. Many fellas got to fuck yourself to fire. Come behind and put a match. Look at your own fire, some people would tell them. Yeah. They all had the clothes like that now. But they had more masks.
Did they have much music on carnival day?

Yeah, yeah. Plenty of music. Plenty of parades. More music in the mountains. Yeah, yeah. More music. Like all the old parades still existent today. The Rakes of Carmel, Porteries. Because I used to watch in them parades.
You used to do what in the parades?
Oh, I used to tote lights. Lead the mules. I was waking up for them. We had to lead all the animals in the parades. Wait for John Everett. Big Teamsters place. A Dramon. Yeah.
Well did they have jazz bands playing in the parades?
Yeah, well like you got a club where you get to hide them bands. Hide them bands.
But I mean Rakes and Comas and Momas.
Oh no, no colored in them parades.
But no jazz bands, no white jazz bands.

Yeah, they had white, they had a few ragtime jazz bands. But most sentimental songs, you know. Yeah. With them parades. No, no other organizations like they got, they did have jazz band music. But them days, white folks had all them big brass bands. Plenty of brass bands. I used to get them from away. I heard the color city used to come from Mississippi. Plenty of them. They had music. They had music. They had music. No colored in the parades.
How could you strut and shake with that big light when they had those brass bands?
Oh, we used to do our number. That was the time. Just hold them lights on. Yeah, that way you get your kicks. Most people look at the light toward in the parade.
Oh sure.

It goes on now. Yeah, it goes on with them days. I used to like it late. Then I would make it money when I used to like the music. The only thing you had time getting one of them lights though. Sometimes you had to fight for them lights. Really? Yeah, those come right from back of Cali up Magnoia. That's where the big den was. Yeah. That's a fight to get in the yard. Once you can get in that yard where you can get a light. But it's to get in that gate. See when they would open the gate a bunch of fellas would shove in. When they had nobody to pull you back. Police and nobody else. When the open night game when they would bring the mules there people comes in. When they get in the yard where you got a chance to work.
Did the people throw money in the streets?
No, no, no. No more than toys. Them little things. I mean to the uh... No money.
To the fellas that had the lights.
They didn't have money for you. No, no money. No, no money.
They do that now sometimes.

Well no they can't. You have to be behind them floats with them lights. Yeah, yeah. You got to watch out with them lights. Yeah. They hire you for their parade. People on the float chose all your little silvonaires. Chose all your little silvonaires to tell you.
Now where did you hear Joe Oliver? You mentioned hearing him.
Well I met him at the Copper Raider Hall. He's one of the good cornet players right behind Manuel Perez. Yeah, he took me at the Copper Raider Hall. An outstanding cornet player going.
Did those cornet players use many mutes? Different kind of things for me?
Yeah, well. Well Joe Oliver most used his doobie. He used it until he died. When he's doobie.
And what about the other fellas?
Well he used to have, used to have things to put in cornet. But I'm talking about Joe Oliver. He had them too, but he used to use that hat most. Yeah, Joe Oliver used to use that big ol' doobie.
You remember a fella they called Freddy Kepard?

Yeah, Freddy Kepard. Yeah, he was good too. He used to use, I went to his dance. Sometime he would play at the Copper Raider. But see, Manuel Perez was outstanding. Him, he couldn't, they couldn't come there. Because they had him contracted all the time. For every dance would come. At the Copper Raider? Yeah, yeah. No, that was at the Columet Hall, Manuel Perez. Freddy Kepard, well he came from, he used to play at the Columet, get in a band. You know if you give him a dance, you get in a band you want.
Did you hear Kepard before the storm?
Well I heard him a couple of times.
You remember that was before the big storm?
What? Freddy Kepard? I heard him before the storm. I heard him before the storm around 1914. I heard him. Yeah, I went to his dance. He was a little bit of a dance.
You remember another cornet player, Bunk Johnson? No. What's that called Bunk?
I know Blue, well I didn't know him good, but I've been behind his music. He's a fella who broke his gall string right down my way, one son behind a parade.
His gall string?
Broke that from blowing, shot him up in the air. In his throat huh? Died that night. They call him Blue. Blue, Walter Blue. Yeah, yeah.
His son plays at Lutton's now. Little Blue is at Lutton's. The old folks on down at Almonaster and Murray.
Yeah, I remember him on Sunday.
What about Buddy Petit?

Well Buddy Petit, he was a good cornet player. He had a contract by the Percy Brinshall. He used to play downtown, Percy Brinshall. He was a good cornet player too, Buddy Petit. Yeah, I knew him good.
Did you ever get across Canal Street to go to any of the dances uptown on Rampart Street?

Well, yeah, I used to go to dances, yeah. I used to go to that Rube Garden. Oh yeah. I used to go to another place on Grabby Street. The way we used to do, we wouldn't have no kind of money to go in the dead. We'd send one fella with my hat. We asked the man to let him take, go see for my hat. The fella did. Oh yeah. We'd go in the dead, you know. But we were small. We didn't have much money them days. But he had plenty of dance there, the Rube Garden. I didn't go to Rube Garden much, but I went on that other garden. I forgot that place on right on Grabby it was.
Near Rampart?
Yeah, near Rampart, upstairs. I forgot the name.
I think that was the garden too, wasn't it? Yeah, yeah.

Yeah, it was the Winter Garden. That's where it was, the Winter Garden. See, the Rube Garden, most of us were sedating than this one on Grabby Street. I'll tell you that. Everybody couldn't hit that Rube Garden like you want. Yeah, not like on Rampart. That was the Winter Garden. That's what it was. Well, you remember them places too.
I heard somebody tell me about it. Yeah. Did the Dances of the Pelican though?
Well, the story, well I didn't go that much. They had dances there, but I didn't go that much.
Who would be playing the dances in these different places uptown?
Well, there had a few new fellas came along playing there.
They wouldn't be the old time downtown guys, huh?

No, no. No, no. Old downtown crowd would be like at the Rube Garden and things. All them head musicians like Frederick Keppard, Joe Oliver, and they would be the old town. But if you keep man your pro race, just like Wooden Joe used to play the downtown in them halls, like the new halls. There were two, three halls down my way. Got them, yeah. They were running. Two, three of them they taught in the church today like the Fronds-Amin. That's right around the corner from the back of my house used to be where I moved from that block. Fronds-Amin, that was a nice place, big hall too. Fronds-Amin. That was a point in them days I couldn't go in that hall much. I was too dark them days.
They wouldn't let you in. The light tree all day.

That's right. Now you're talking. They wouldn't let you in though. As we wouldn't go, but we'd know what it is. See, they had to let us go in. Because folks used to go in, but we always didn't know what kind of all it was. Yeah. But I stayed down there all my day. That's right, like Creole.
Did you know the Creole language? Did you know that?

No, I never used to say. I'm Creole, but I never used to talk. Just a few little boys. Bonsoir. Bonsoir, and what else you say? Well, like Bonsoir. Bonsoir. Bonsoir. Bonsoir. Bonsoir. Bonsoir. Bonsoir. I didn't know something about it.
How do you say, how do you do in Creole?
Yes. Suppose you meet somebody, what you say? I'll be that Bonsoir. I see.
Who were some of the outstanding drummers when you were young?

Well, well with Bob and Bob Aran and a little fella called Little Sheik used to play at the palace. He used to call him. And Little Big Big. I know you know him. He plays up and down all the time. Chinese Big Big.
Oh yeah.
Yeah, he is a good drum player.
Little Sheik used to play at the palace, huh?
Sheik, yeah. Sheik. That ain't the way to call him. This is, oh what's his name? He come up with Bob Barber and that he come up with. Yeah, happy. Happy.
What color is that?
Oh, he's a bright fella.
That'd be red happy then they call him.
Yeah. You know there's two of them. Yeah, he used to take a drum truck there and beat it and show them sticks. Oh, he used to be at the palace theater here.
Who had the band there, do you remember?
I don't know who had the band, but I know the drum player was happy.
Did you ever hear John Robichaux's band?

Well I heard them, that's in my daddy time. They used to play at the Artfeller Hall, you know, they're at the Artfeller Hall by the basin. I was pretty small them days. That's my daddy time, them band Robichaux.
Was Lincoln Park, when you were a boy, was Lincoln Park running? Here comes another one of those.
Where Lincoln Park? I heard about Lincoln Park all my days, me. Was it running? Did you ever go out there? Well I never went out. What you mean, out on the lake, yeah?
No, no, no.
Oh you mean, all that Lincoln Park? Way up on Colton, Broad. Yeah, I thought, I didn't mean this, I mean up on Broad. Well I never go up there much, I went up there once.
It was running already?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, it was running, yeah. It's old park, it's been running.
How old were you? How old were you?
Oh, me?
When you went to Lincoln Park?

Oh man, I went there once and I never forget, see a ball game. I went to ball game, that's years ago though. Were you in short pants? Yeah, I was in short pants, yeah. I was about 12 years old then, yeah.
Did your daddy ever tell you about uh, different uh bands he heard or places he went?

Well I'm telling you, he had told me plenty, but not too many bands, but like that old band, because they used to keep him at his hall, at the Longshoremen Hall. It wasn't Longshoremen, our fellas hall. Who would that be? That was right on Toulouse and Basin. That's when they had the schooners, you don't know that, they had the schooners there, the old basin. See, all that was nothing but water back there from Toulouse and Basin, you know that Basin Street?
Yeah, went all the way back to the canal, all over there?

Went all the way to the uh, all the way to the uh, to the Bayer there, to the Bayer. Right there the Auditorium. Yeah, yeah, that's where all the Chaco used to come in. After they did it with that, where the Chaco used to come in, come in through the by railroad call, but they used to come by schooners. Come there and come in the new canal basin.
And what band was this your daddy used to listen to? Did he tell you the name of it?
Uh, no, I was small when he used to go to dances and things. He didn't tell you much about it? No, no. But you did say Robichard was back in that time? Yeah, yeah, Robichard was back in that time.
Did you ever hear him talk about Buddy Bolden?

Well, yeah, I didn't hear my dad used to talk about Buddy Bolden. Why don't you please come home? Yeah, yeah, that was a little bit of thing then. He knew nothing much about dance, but I would talk of him.
Do you remember Louis Armstrong when he started out?

Did you ever hear him talk about him? Well, I'll tell you. Well, I'll tell you about Louis Armstrong. He just, when he first come out, I heard about him, but I don't know when he started out, but I heard them fellas. Now you had to see, see, he come up with this fella on Bourbon Street. Now you call him Papa Celestine, learned them plenty. And then I heard about Joe Oliver who had learned them coming up. But the Petey, see you understand, the one took them out around them nightclubs and things. He the one gave me to start them out. Down there, the rural house was open up around Iperville Basin Street. Oh, yeah.
You remember the district when it was running up here?

Well, yeah, I just had to put on long pants. It was closing up then. Yeah, yeah, I used to go through them then, but I had to put on long pants them days too. I just had to get on long pants when they did away with it.
You say you knew Lawrence too, huh, and his brothers?
Yeah, Simon. He used to play bass, Simon Moray.
What kind of a bass player was he?
One of these.
Yeah, but I mean, was he good?

Was he good? Yeah, he was one of the wonderful. He the one played with, he used to play with, uh, he played with, uh, with Manuel Wilde, but his daddy was the main man with him. His dad was with Manuel, with him though, Simon's daddy. He used to call him Bill Moray. He was short, fella. He was like Lawrence. He called him Bill Moray.
He was short too, I know him.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, he was short. I know them good. I know the whole family of them because I used to go to school with him on the village and I used to pass their corner all the time.
What about, uh, John?
John, well, he was a guitar player here. I know John, he died too, huh?
Yeah, up in New York.

Yeah, yeah, yeah, he was one of the good guitar players. Well, John went away from a bar when I was, when John left here. But Simon always just, uh, uh, Simon. Well, Lauren had a whole lot of other bands. His cousin in them started taking bands. You was Neely, you know who he talked about Neely, his cousin played clarinet?
I know him well.
Yeah.
Who did he play with?

Well, I just did. I want to tell you, he used to come around with Louis and Joe and them. I know plenty of musicians and, uh, I can't call their name because I know that little guitar player used to stay like Desvin. I used to know him. I just forgot about them. He was a good cornet, uh, cornet player, Desvin. Yeah, he kind of was new, him.
Yeah, I knew they'd been there, but they used to be one of the, one of the men of the, of French singing they had. Nothing but nice singing they had, French.
Do you remember when it burned down?
Well, I just can't place it at this moment.
I think I remember the date. I mean, were you around?
Yeah, we talked about it. Yeah, yeah. I didn't come around.
It was 1919, I believe.

No, no. No, it burned down way around, let me see, where this place is burned there around the corner, 1910. It must have burned down around, I believe it went down right around the stone. It went down around 15, 1915.
Did you see the fire? Do you remember?
No, I remember what I was talking about, but I didn't come up to see it. But that was the time it was going on.
Did you ever know any of the musicians that worked there? I think it was mostly a white band, of course.

Yeah, yeah, I didn't know much of the musicians there. The reason I didn't go to that show, because it was most French. French opera, nothing but French. That's the real time they really had the French. The same way they had the theater. You want to talk about the theater? About the theater, the Dolphin Theater. Used to have bowler shows. That was my daddy's time. I couldn't go to them shows. But that was some of the wonderful days, them days, of the day. Because today you couldn't have them with the young generation coming up, them kind of shows. You couldn't have them. What's going on? Well, you know, young folk cheering all how they is today. The ambition, they be more ambitious, I think, you know. And then them days, we were small, we couldn't go to them. It was just for men to go in them shows. Yeah, we couldn't go to them. What you call a bowler, they don't have them anymore. Give them a set of time about Bechet. Who did he bum around? Bechet? Well, he was one of them good old clarinet players. He come out with his uncle and that was the Imperial Band. When they had Mani Parade with the Superior Band, they had the Imperial Band. Yeah, that was Bechet. Sitting in the Dead Band. He knows. Yeah, yeah. He used to stay around my house too. Yeah, all of them come from around the 7th Ward.
Do you remember when they started using San Jacinto Hall for when they built it?

Well, yeah. Well, yeah. I remember they made a big club out of it when they built it. Yeah, they were building it. It was a club, society. My uncle used to be in it. I never did be in it. It was a wonderful club that was.
Did you ever know which bands played there? Did Sidney Desvina, I know, played there for a while?

Yeah, yeah. Yeah, they played there. Any other bands that you know of? Yeah, Sidney played there. Buddy Petit played there plenty too. Yeah, Buddy Petit played there plenty. What was he like? Did you know Buddy very well? Buddy Petit? Well, I knew him. He was a little older than me, but I had a bum with him, but I knew him. Yeah. About going to the dances and things. What did he look like? Little brown-skinned fella. Short brown-skinned fella. What about Chris Kelly? Well, Chris Kelly, he was another good player, but I didn't know him too much. Sam Morgan in those? Yeah, I know Sam Morgan. He came from down below. Yeah, he used to play at the Do you remember the Cooperators Hall? Was that called Hope's Hall? Hope's Hall, that's it. They changed the name? Yeah, they changed the name on the Late Watch. Yeah, yeah, with the Hope Hall. On the Late Watch? Well, I mean years after. Late years, I see. Yeah, years after. Yeah, yeah, with the Hope Hall. They had the Society too there. Oh, uh, that's... And the Bonkays I used to go there. What's a Bonkay? Bonkays, that's just like a dance. That's like a party. Everybody couldn't go in there. You had to be in the Society or they'd give you one invitation to bring a friend. Yeah. That was something too. Anything to eat much? Oh, plenty to eat. Plenty to eat and drink. Yeah, that was just like Saturday. Bonkays better than a dance because everything was free.
But what happened at first in the Bonkays? Well, it'd be a Society. No, I mean when you first come to it,

what did you do first? Go to dancing. You danced first? Yeah, because we'd go around there when the dance would... music started at one o'clock and they played until six o'clock in the evening. And then she's over. Yeah, you go there when they dance. Well, they were at night. They were in the evening? No, in the evening. In the daytime it was. Well, how... Daytime Bonkays were. How long would you dance? From one to six. Well, when did you do your evening? Well, they'd start between. If you want a little sandwich, a little place, you go in the kitchen and get something to eat, they give you. Most people went there to dance, my dear, and drink. More for dancing. More for dancing. Dancing and drinking. Plenty of beer and wine. They had lemonade and things too there. Yeah. Did people drink in New Orleans in those days? Oh, they did. They swallowed. Yes, indeed. They drank. They never started drinking. They weren't so when the beer went, when the liquor went on to exist, they went to making homebrew.
They were going to get it during the morning. They make their own beer. Yeah, make their own beer. Any of them have skills? Did they do any distilling through moonshine?

No, we used to make it too, at all. I don't know. We'd make it, put it up, and have to leave it for four or five days, then you go to put it in your bottle. You get a cap, then after you put it in the bottle, you leave it there for about... Well, some folks leave it for a day, and then they go to say, light the cap to that evening to drink it.
Somebody told me once that Shots, did you know Shots Madison or Kid Shots? That was a, he used to sell homebrew. That was his main job, I think, during Prohibition. Yeah. But Fess told us. Yeah.
Well, you know, Kid Ernest was in that sometimes too.
Did you know Shots, he was uptown.
He lived in the battlefield. Yeah.
He lived up on Cleveland. Yeah, I know the battlefield.
He played in all the parades, and not all of them a lot of times.
Yeah. Yeah, we used to make it. Good beer, homebrew. Take time to make it, but when you make it, you enjoy it.
Well, you can still get good corn whiskey from Mississippi.
Yeah, yeah. But you see it, see the Stricon liquor up this day from another place like that. Corn whiskey and things.
Did you get that during the Prohibition times here?

Well, yeah, you get sometime in them speakeasies. Used to have a place called in the Barney to be speakeasy. You have to know them horses to go in and knock at. Yeah. They get in. Yeah, because they're Stricon. Speakeasy.
What were some of the famous speakeasies here?
Well, I don't know. I called them all hole in the wall.
Did they have bands in there?

No. Nothing with Drake. You couldn't make no noise. You couldn't yell this toward it. Why don't you be quiet? You make noise, it'll show you out. See, the Lord be looking for all that. They call it speakeasy. It's supposed to speak low.
Well, that's a good idea. I wish they'd do that today in the morning.

Oh, yeah. You couldn't speak like in a barroom the day with music and all that. And I would speak easy. If you make noise, talk loud. It'll put you out if you're out of place. You got to be easy talking. Easy. Nobody knows. Because they forbid you to sell that stuff. You just feel like drinking. You know where it's at. Just go. I had uncle had one, but a police didn't come there with his face black and in the daytime. My uncle was there today and his partner was there at night. Come right there and rested him.
A white policeman? For sure.

How you going to get them to them speakeasy? I'm sure you're a white policeman. They're just black in his face. Well, they don't do it. Police don't do it like they did years ago, like higher aggressive and thing. You're writing out, writing the paper. You put on clothes to catch your teeth, being churches and all that. Put on clothes like a woman. Them dead police and black in their face. Come there and drink with them fellas. They're just an old head. You know, buying the liquor. That night he come there, he got you. He's been there already. Yeah. All right, uncle had to speak of that car. He didn't rest in, but he was on his day. The man drink with him that day, but that night they called his partner. Yeah. They got off. They're fine. They got off. Just trying to break it up. That's the only thing when the kitchen was. You got to watch out. You had to be on your whole time. Yeah, to be on your whole time in the kitchen.
Do you remember many picnics when you were young? Did they give picnics in the country?
Oh yeah, at the fairground. That's where all the picnic was. Right out the fairground. Not a good place. Entertainment. What would they do at a picnic? Dancing, playing the music.
Well, how would they dance? Would they spread anything on the ground? No, they're dancing.
It's a big open place. Never been in that fairground?
Well, no, I don't know the place. Or the race.

Yeah, yeah. On the ground. College used to have that more than the white folks today one time. In my round, 1825. From 18 to 25, it was all a picnic. See all them holidays like old soldier did. I was labor day. And art fella day. There was every year a parade be coming. There was about five or six different parades. That's all I used to go to the fairground. That's the biggest place to hold the people them days. Fairground.
Well, how many bands would they have?

Oh, they would have two. They have a Sedaton band. You know, a Selen Matters band. And a Ragtime band be out in the field on the platform. You know, we'd be out there dancing. That's the Ragtime band. Nothing but drags. But the other ones, all that slow drag. And everything is out there shaking and thick. Yeah. Oh, that was something that's fairground. Yeah, that's fairground.
Would they drink much at the picnic?
See, I wouldn't go to work that day just to go to picnic. Better go sometime, go in the evening. I'll come back till 2, 3 o'clock in the morning.
Eat?
Mostly picnic being for the children that day, but at nighttime for the big people. And they stay open from 8 to 4 o'clock in the morning, picnic all night.
What'd they eat?

Oh, yeah, eating and drinking. Plenty of eating. Plenty of eating, plenty of drinking. Plenty of entertainment they had. That's why I first learned, rode automobile. Cost me about $4 one evening. That's the road automobile of my life. Cost me $4. Diamond ride. Right around. That's a diamond ride. I would meet a girl. I wouldn't know her something. I'd treat her. That's a right ride. Yeah.
How much for each ride?
Ten cents.
Well, you spent $4?

Yeah, you don't ride too far. No. It's a ride they give you. Yeah. But we're so glad. We didn't know what cars were. We were riding an automobile every day. They had flying horses and all that. All kind of entertainment. Plenty of music, nice music.
I was going to ask about lawn parties too.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, I used to go to lawn parties up on Taylor Street. I called the lady, called Miss Cole. Yeah, they used to have plenty of lawn parties going on. Every Sunday, they used to have parties. And what I say, they can't have that today on account of the young generation. Too rough. My days, they have all kind of nice parties. Have somewhere to go on Sunday. Just like the lake. You heard talk about Mill and Boy. That was the best place for the colored people to go. That's all the place we had one time. Mill and Boy. Yeah. It was better than I got Lincoln Beach. Mill and Boy was nice.
A lot of colored went out there. We had Mill and Boy.

Yeah, that's where Frederick Cappy used to play music too. And Buddy Petit and them out there. They have a big dance hall there. Yeah. All the colors used to have. That little train used to run. Little Smokey Mary. Used to be on Legion Field. Catch a ride chest sometimes on Legion Field and Canal. I mean on Canal by the river. But most times you had to go to Legion Field and St. Gordon catch it. And go right on by 15 cents. Get you right on the train.
And what went on out at the lake?
Plenty of dancing. Fishing. Everything. Plenty of entertainment.
Were there places you could pay to go in?
Well yeah. Well yeah. Sometime had dance hall. You know the dance hall be out on the water. Wouldn't cost much. Two bits. Sometime 15 cents. But you had to pay to go in.
Would they have any comedians or show girls dancing?
No they had no show. Yeah they had some place to have show girls.
Where would that be?
Out on the lake.
Would they do that in town here?

Well no they used to do it on the lake. Out on the lake. They could do the singing. But that's when they didn't have a concert or nothing. But they used to be out on the lake. That's the only place people had to go. Culling on Sundays. The milling boys. The milling boys. The only place they had. The Lincoln Park. I didn't go up that much. But I always talk of it. Well now. At these dances they wouldn't have had intermission or something like that.
They wouldn't have anybody else come in like dancing girls or comedians or anything?
Oh yeah. Oh no. No they'd have to hire a couple of them to do that.
They'd hire them?
Yeah yeah.
And what would they do?
Be singing. Gang of blues and things singing.
Who'd sing the blues here then?
Well I know the one girl I call Alice. She used to sing.
Alice huh?
Mm-hmm. That was her name. You remember any of the songs you sang? No I didn't know him. I know where he was from downtown. From like a place.
This girl was from downtown?
Yeah this girl was from down and back. She used to sing out the lake. That was her job. Just like an actor. Is she still around? From from. No I believe she died that girl.
Who'd she sing with?

Sing by herself. And they had another girl too used to sing. I don't believe her sister used to sing. She had a sister but I used to see her singing. I know that. I see the fella used to be her husband now and then. He's living where Alice had died then.
You want to ask him about it and let us know. Appreciate it.
Did you ever hear um.
I'm gonna bring my real boy here to talk for y'all about the music.
Who's that?
That's my boy George. He played with uh. He used to play about a peda.
What does he play with?
Oh he played guitar. George we called him George.
That guy with big bushy eyebrows? I believe so. Joey Gino? I believe so.

Is on Roman? He's kind to uh. I don't know where he's the he's kind. He was kind to the days being in there. Richie in there. I know him good. I see him. He's pretty nice as well. I see him. Yeah he played on Burden Street.
Yeah we know him. We have talked to him already.
Yeah.
This is George Gino.
We'll show you a picture of it. Yeah.
You got a picture now?
Yeah well ask him.
Yeah I'll get it just now.
He used to be with my other boy. They played clarinet over there. About uh. Pat out.
Well this isn't a very big picture. Does that look like him down there?
Oh no he's bright in there. He's a bright fella. Oh this is oh this is George uh.
Gino they call him.

No the one playing clarinet. He's still on Orleans Street. What that fella used to play by the Pat out? I know him there too George. He's a pretty good guy. George Lewis? George Lewis. Me and Mr. Bum together. Oh yeah sure George. I know George Lewis. He used to play with uh. He played with Miele in there man. George Lewis.
I wanted to ask you to get back to the lawn parties again. Did they charge charge something to get in the lawn party?
Yeah yeah yeah yeah. Charged you two bits. 25 cents. Yeah I had to pay to go in the party. I had to pay to go in the party.
And to have drinks so much?
Yeah I had drink. Ten cents a glass.
Glass of what?
Well they had wine beer. But most of them days they had we called it beer but we know it'd be that home brew. In that beer you can go to the beer them days and get it. Put up these beer. Home brew.
Home brew. Yeah. How was the dancing? Was it right on the ground or?
Yeah on the ground. Mud ground. Mud ground.
Have you ever put down?
Some of them would put on napoleon. Tapoleon down. Oh yeah. Some of them would put that down.
Have you ever had wood boards?
No no no wood boards. No no wood boards.
Where did the bands sit? Did they have a little bandstand or how were they?
No.
Where'd they put the bands?
The bands be sitting over with some chairs and things. Right on the ground? On the ground. They got one of them big parties right four doors of my house tonight. One of them old time parties.
Really? Tonight?
Yeah tonight.
Long parties. Oh god.
Where do you live now by the way? Out of 2040.
That's the same old neighborhood.
You ought to have this over there. Now that way you get some of these little new bands. They good with the little new bands.
Young kids huh?

Yeah they pretty good. Yeah about four doors of my house. They'd been going no appetite for the last two months. They don't have that much no more. No. I never see them. Well you can see this one. You had a car you can just drive around there. I would see I'd bring you in there and be glad when you come in and buy one or two grass of beer make of self.
I gotta go to a party tonight and I can't go. I gotta go across the river.
I think it might stop there though earlier. What time is that?

Oh that party? Oh now I'm gonna be straight. That party around my house they start from 8 till late. They'll be there 2-3 o'clock in the morning. Because they have permit and all that you know. They might have policemen there. Parties now they gotta get policemen. Yeah they usually do. Yeah they gotta get policemen. They keep them quiet. I'd like to get some good pictures of the long parties. You sure? There'd be one good for the night. Yeah. These pictures. There'd be one good. You know I had an often down there. They had one about a tree months ago. I told a girl myself I might come buy a tree. But I don't go there before. I got no other people too you know. I don't know who give me some clothes. I know the people in the house where they sometimes they rent the people yard you know. Yeah. It's in a big yard.
Yeah it's fixing it up just now. What is the address about?
The part is in the 20-hundred block.
On Polgar?

Mm-hmm. It's right by that school. You see that big school. I stay in the cross-street from that school on Polgar. Between Vera and Oakwood. You pass that block you're not there you hear that music. Mm-hmm. You hear that music there. You stay in the corner you hear it.
Well what else went on at those lawn parties? They had music and dancing and drinking?
Well music and dancing, yeah.
Any gambling?
Nine then, oh no they had dancing, no party. No, no.
You gonna say nine then?
No I mean uh I would say nine then they would have little prizes given away. Uh-huh.
What would that be?
For the best dancer.
Uh-huh. And what would they give them?

Some of them give them a little presents, some of them give them money. About five dollars. All of them. But they did have parties all give all that. Just come to the parties. They want you to come in, barge and dance, enjoy yourself. Dance and eat. That's the way the party goes today.
Have you been to Fish Fry?
Oh yeah, Fish Fry. Yeah well, Fish Fry don't have no music or nothing. Fish Fry. It's just entertainment amongst your friends. No music in Fish Fry. No music in Fish Fry. No music in Fish Fry.
In the old days? No. They didn't have a piano player or?
Well they had some houses you catch, piano player. Now I know one of the good piano players he did, that was Pelabon. You might have heard of him Pelabon, Eugene Pelabon.
Eugene Pelabon. Eugene Pelabon.
Yeah, he was a good piano player. I know Pichon too is a good piano player. He used to stay on the clay bone a few blocks of my heart.
What kind of number did Pelabon feature?

Oh, plenty of blues. He played music with his foot and all that. With his feet and all that. Just a minute back. Yeah. He used to play music with his feet. Sit on on the back side and play piano. That's piano pretty good.
He played piano with his feet?
Yeah, with his feet.
Yeah, with his feet. My brother used to do it, but he could only hit one base.
Yeah, but Pelabon used to do it.
He could play a tune that way?
Yeah, he was dead him, but he was a people living.
Where did his people live?
Well, these people was living in the Trammare. These people was living.
I think I know a guy named Pelabon down there.
What the hell? Lawrence and all of them when he was living with them. He was well known for 27th. And Pichu, well I knew him, but I'd have left his bum with him because he played piano nicely.
Who's that? Pichon, Walter.
Walter Pichon, he's a nice piano player.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
But do they have any of these little serenading groups walking around from door to door? Did you ever hear any of those?
What, music?
Yeah, serenading, you know, they call it.
Like these there around by Ron St. Peter Street, them boys?
Mm-hmm.

Playing? Yeah. Well, they had a few of them. Well, they had a couple of them at parties like that. They wasn't really musicians. They just make up a band. One time they didn't have, you ever take notice they had harmonicas and uh, and they had that whistle they used to blow. Them fellas used to take them whistles and lack of music. I don't know if you ever heard them whistles. You put them out. Play music with them whistles. Did that slide?
Did you change that?
No, no. I didn't mean that. Tune on it? No, just a little whistle about that big. You put underneath your tongue.
Oh, I've...

See, I can blow them. Yeah, I know. But I know fellas them days to make music out and you could dance by them. I know a white fella today. I don't believe he died in Hamilton, huh? Hamilton. Hamilton. Walter Hamilton. That judge himself. He used to play there.
He'd come up down my way.

Yeah, he used to play. Could dance by them music. A little whistle ahead. I don't see him no more. A little bit of whistle. Put it on your tongue. You used to blow it like with a... But them fellas used to make music out them. And harmonicas. That's what they used to dance by too one time. Harmonica. Good.
This guy was a judge that blew that whistle you knew, huh?

Yeah, Hamilton. Yeah. Walter. I believe it was Walter Hamilton. He'd come from around St. Natin and Fury around my house. I remember when they was in Short Pants, they'd be all around the bar playing them music. Playing them whistles. I know them colored boys, they had a little party. They'd come in there with that band, with that little whistle. And some would come with a harmonica. And like you say, some of them would add that whistle like a flute too. They'd take a can read and put on it and make like a whistle. Can read.
I guess they made a lot of things at home.
Oh yeah. A fella would make things that fixed that to make music.
You ever hear any good rub board players?
Well, no. I worked one rubble at the Palace Theater.
Yeah?

What? Well they come there. Now just like that other great musician I see at the Palace with that one leg. Played by 10 instruments. He comes there. Cornet, strong, trombone, and he had all that on the stage. Tell me to come from over the river, I know his name. He's a pig lake fellow to play music. Yeah, I know his name.
That beats me.
Yeah, he was at the Palace. Not at the Palace. I thought of touring. He come here on, uh, he come here on Lionel, Lionel show.
Lionel Hampton?
Yeah, you remember when they come here. I went to his show. I went...
Like Bates, could that be it?

He's from over the river, they say, but he's up north now. He with them. Yeah, I went to all of them when they came here, man. Caught me four and a half to see Louis Armstrong, and four and a nine, eight, twice. I ain't gonna pay no more. Yeah, they was at the auditorium, Louis Armstrong, I see, Lionel Hampton. It was a packed house, but I tell you, they went there most for that little son to come there, but his son didn't shoot up, Lionel Hampton. I seen Night King Cole.
Well, I just forgot to ask, I started to ask, did you ever know Ann Cook uptown?

Well, I heard talk about Ann Cook. Well, I don't know that Ann Cook used to sell. That Ann Cook used to sing and she used to sell macho, you know, mean fools around in boats on the river. Maybe. Ann Cook. Yeah, she used to stay uptown around Grabby or Padilla Street. She used to stay.
She was a hospital.
Yeah, yeah, that's what I'm telling you, but she was a working person. Yeah, Ann Cook. Yeah.
Did you ever work on any of the boats or around on the docks? Any of the...
Well, yeah. Well, I didn't work on them, but I used to haul from them, see, because I was driving my days. I used to drive big...
Was there much music down there? Did the fellas sing blues or anything or...
Well, yeah, there plenty of them used to sing blues. I used to do plenty of them. Mmm.
Would they have any musical instrument with them when they sang?
No.
Just sing, huh?
Some of them have guitars. That's all I sing with a guitar.
You don't remember the songs they sang, any of that, huh?
Well, I heard them sing Sworn the River one of them.

I wonder, do you remember in unloading the boats, did they ever, or lifting coffee sacks or anything, did they ever have any little songs they'd sing or rhythms they'd go through, you know, to do it together to work?

No, I heard them fellas on the railroad do that. What did they do on the railroad? Huh? What'd they do on the railroad? Well, they'd be picking and singing. I don't know how to sing with Isaiah Young, though. Picking and singing. All kinds of stuff.
You never saw them do that and unload coffee?
No, no, not coating the coffee and thing. I didn't see them unload coffee.
George Lewis once told me that he used to do that. They had four of them together.

Well, I guess among them. They started singing. It looked like them big boats. They don't hear that no more there. The big old steam of grace. You might heard of that. The Tennessee bell and all that. Well, that was roustabout boats. I had to bring stuff there. Fellas throw all that stuff off the wall on the shore and go load up the boat. They'd be singing. They'd call it roustabout.
They'd be singing that.

Yeah, they didn't hear this old president boat yet, them days. You see, I remember when all that was closed in, I used to drive them days. I used to drive them. I used to drive them mules and wagons for a train for them. All that was closed in. It used to come from way up in Colton. Clean on down to Espinade. That's the foyer that she was laying. All the rest of that shed had been built lately, mostly after the wall. But up to Espinade, it's the Mandible Street wall. The foyer that most you can go. Outside they had the banana boat. But I mean, come down through the wall. I mean, through the wall. Walking down there. You can't do that no more. You got partition now between them wall. They used to be right open. You can walk side of the wall all the way down time. You used to can come. Right chain, yeah, side of the wall. Yeah, they didn't have no prison in the boat.
Did you ever go on any excursions?

Oh yeah, excursions. Yeah, I went plenty of excursions. Yeah, I used to have them all the time on the Shelby Road. I used to be on a little railroad, you know, St. Lord Street. Bring it on to St. Silp, all the way down the country, from the head. Yeah. That way I used to hear some nice music too. But I used to be on that. Be on the train playing that music. You just have to tell them, play some music. Be playing until they get on where they going at. Yeah, they'd make excursions.
Could you dance on excursions?

No, they'd be on the train. Couldn't dance until you get on where they going at. They'd be on the train playing music. Yeah, when you get to the place where they going at, where they have a big hall. Yeah, that's where everybody go down there. Having their fun. Some people just go down there for the ride. That's all. Yeah, plenty of excursions I went on. Well, that's where they used to have fights at on them. Explorations. Shoo. Plenty of fights. Dang. Yeah, plenty of fights. Plenty of fights at one of the excursions I used to have. I remember they had a fight on the train. They on the train would come. They'd be done ring up the law and tell them to wait at the depot. They'd be on the train catching right there. They had a fight right on the train. Somebody done got off the train and ringed up that quick. You had to be fighting on the train. I see my mother was on one up. Never no more she went. They had a fight cutting up.
When they had the band on the train, where did they have dancing?
No, not on the train. They just would play music.
Somebody told me once they'd have the baggage car or something. A little dance floor.
No, no dancing. They couldn't dance on the train. Where did the band play? Yeah, the band played. Yeah, they played gang of tunes until they gone where they going at.
Where were they? In the coach?

They'd be in the coach. In the coach. In the coach. In the coach. Yeah, they'd be in the coach with all the instruments among themselves. Yeah, when they get where they going at then they start to play dancing. Yeah, that excursion was nice. Excursion and going to the lake. That's the only thing they had good.
Where did you know Danny from?

Well, I just knew them. She was my girl, daughter Mary. Her sister, his wife's sister is my girl daughter, father-in-law. See, you know Augie, you never met little Augie, Miss Louise Boyd. I had Johnny all of them back there one day. You know when I used to come by Johnny, I used to drink. I had him and him, Hall, Jack. You remember when they? They all brought me back there. Come sit on the garage and everything. But they didn't know I was like you. I brought them back there. They tried to bring my little girl's little grandchild to draw his picture. I never did bring them. Yeah, they all came back there.
Did you ever hear Danny play music?
I didn't know him around there. I stood up there once or twice.
Where's that?
